On this enquiry from Raghava, the two disciples of the Sage

"The blessed Valmiki, who is attending the sacrifice, is the 
author of the poem in which thine whole life is told. Twenty-
four thousand verses and a hundred Upakhyanas1 have been 
used by that ascetic, the son of Bhtigu. • Five hundred Sargas

Thy 
conduct, thy circumstances, thine entire life is unrolled with its 
vicissitudes. If thou desirest it, 0 King, thou mayest hear it 
from us in the intervals of the sacrifice, in thy moments of leisure. 
Thereafter Ramo, accompanied by the Sages and magnanimous 
monarchs, having heard that melodious chant, returned to the 
sacrificial pavilion. 
That recitation accompanied by Talas and Layas, • divided into 
Sargas in harmonious notes and tones, in which the scansion was 
stressed by the stringed instruments, was heard by the King

At this extremely significant command from Raghava, the

" 0 Blessed Ones, with your disciples, the kings and their

These words of the magnanimous Raghava were praised by all

" Such conduct is only possible in Thee and is found nowhere 
else in the world, 0 Prince ! " 
Having resolved thus, Raghava, the Scourge of his Foes,

" To-morrow this shall take place," whereupon he dismissed

brief.summary_1line: Rama, realizing the singers are Sita’s sons, orders that Sita appear before the assembly to publicly swear and prove her purity.

image_candidates.scene_text: In a crowded sacrificial assembly of sages and kings, Rama listens intently as the young twins Kusha and Lava sing the epic of his own life.
Rama, seated among sages and monarchs, solemnly commands messengers to summon Sita to prove her purity before the gathered assembly.
Royal messengers bow before the radiant sage Valmiki in the forest hermitage as they deliver Rama’s request regarding Sita.

deep.rich_summary: While Rama attends the great sacrifice, the young ascetic singers Kusha and Lava recite a magnificent epic recounting Rama’s own life. When offered gold, they refuse it, explaining that ascetics who live on fruits and roots have no need for wealth. Intrigued, Rama asks about the poem and learns that the sage Valmiki composed it—twenty‑four thousand verses narrating his entire life. As the chanting continues over several days, Rama gradually realizes that the boys are Sita’s sons. Reflecting deeply, he sends messengers to Valmiki requesting that Sita appear and publicly attest to her purity before the assembled sages and kings. Valmiki agrees. Rama announces that on the following day Sita will swear her oath before the great assembly, setting the stage for a decisive and emotionally charged moment in the epic.

highlight_spans.why: Kusha and Lava reject gold and declare the ascetic ideal of living on fruits and roots, revealing their character and surprising Rama’s court.
The boys reveal that Valmiki composed the epic recounting Rama’s entire life, framing the Ramayana as a story within the story.
Rama listens to the song of his life and realizes the singers are Sita’s sons, a quiet but powerful emotional recognition.
Rama sends word that Sita must appear before the assembly to swear to her purity, initiating the dramatic final test.

top_scenes.scene_text: In the sacrificial pavilion, the young ascetics Kusha and Lava sing the Ramayana with stringed instruments while Rama, surrounded by sages, kings, and monkeys, listens in astonishment.
Royal messengers bow before the radiant sage Valmiki in his forest hermitage, delivering Rama’s request that Sita appear and swear her purity.
Rama stands before a vast assembly of sages and kings, announcing that Sita will come at dawn to take a solemn oath of purity before them all.
